texte:
Why your banker smiles when you say "I don't know anything about investing."

Entry fees, 2% a year whether the fund wins or loses, and a simple index fund at about 0.2%. On 10,000 euros over 20 years, the gap can reach around 10,000 euros.

One question before you sign anything: how much does this cost me?

#investingtips #fees #personalfinance
script: Why does your banker smile when you say: I don't know anything about investing?
Most people think it's because bankers are just friendly.
But that sentence is music to their ears.
Because now they can suggest the bank's own funds.
Some charge entry fees of up to three, sometimes five percent, just for walking in.
Then around two percent every single year, whether the fund wins or loses.
A simple index fund often costs about zero point two percent.
On ten thousand euros over twenty years, that gap can grow to around ten thousand euros.
Not stolen. Just politely collected, year after year.
So next time, ask one question first: how much does this cost me?

texte:
Could one billion euros stop a speeding truck?

Ten million 100-euro notes, about ten tonnes of paper. A loaded truck at 90 km/h. We did the maths.

Send this to the friend who asks the weirdest questions.

#money #whatif #funfacts
script: Could a pile of one billion euros stop a speeding truck?
A hundred euro note weighs about one gram.
So a billion euros in hundreds is ten million notes, around ten tonnes of paper.
Stacked flat, they would make a tower more than a kilometre tall.
But packed into a cube, it's a block only about two metres wide.
Now, a loaded truck can weigh forty tonnes.
At ninety kilometres an hour, it slams into the block with four times its weight.
The bundles burst, and money explodes everywhere.
The truck slows down, but it doesn't stop.
So a billion euros can't stop a truck. But it would definitely stop the traffic.

texte:
Your investment fees are a roommate who eats from your fridge. Every single year.

2% sounds tiny. But he eats 2% of everything in the fridge, market up or down. Over 30 years, that's over 40% of what you could have had.

Check how hungry your roommate is. Save this.

#fees #investing #personalfinance
script: What if your investment fees were a roommate who eats from your fridge?
Two percent a year sounds like nothing.
Just a little bite of cheese. Who cares?
But he comes back every single year.
And he doesn't eat two percent of what you put in. He eats two percent of everything in the fridge.
So the fuller your fridge gets, the bigger his bites.
Start with ten thousand euros, wait thirty years, and he has eaten over forty percent of what you could have had.
Market up? He eats. Market down? He still eats.
And he has never bought a single grocery.
So before you sign anything, check how hungry your roommate is.

texte:
Inflation is a shrink ray pointed at your shopping cart.

At 3% a year, 100 euros loses about a quarter of its buying power in ten years. Cash under the mattress gets zapped too.

Follow for one money idea a day, explained in 40 seconds.

#inflation #personalfinance #moneytips
script: What if inflation was a shrink ray, pointed at your shopping cart?
Every year it zaps your money, and the same twenty euros buys a little less.
At two percent a year, you barely notice.
But in October 2022, inflation in the eurozone hit over ten percent.
Suddenly, the cart shrinks fast enough to see.
And here's the sneaky part: cash hidden under your mattress gets zapped too.
At three percent a year, a hundred euros loses about a quarter of its buying power in ten years.
So the money you never touch is the money that shrinks the most quietly.

texte:
What really happens when you hit "sell" in a panic.

Every seller needs a buyer. While you get out, someone calm is buying your shares on sale. Then you pay more to get back in.

Save this for your next bad day on the market.

#investing #stockmarket #psychology
script: What really happens when you hit sell in a panic?
The market drops ten percent, and your brain screams: get out!
So you sell. Instant relief.
But every seller needs a buyer.
On the other side, a calm investor is happily buying your shares on sale.
Then the market recovers, like broad markets have after every crash so far.
And now you're outside, watching through the window.
To get back in, you have to pay more than you sold for.
So panic selling doesn't avoid a loss. It turns a temporary dip into a permanent one.

texte:
What if a country just printed money forever?

Germany 1923: a loaf of bread reached around 200 billion marks. Zimbabwe 2009: a 100 trillion dollar note. Everyone became a billionaire who couldn't afford bread.

Send this to whoever says "just print more money."

#inflation #economics #moneyhistory
script: What would happen if a country just printed money forever?
Everyone would be rich, right?
But money is only worth what it can buy.
Print more notes, and the same loaf of bread needs more of them.
In Germany in 1923, a loaf of bread reached around two hundred billion marks.
People carried cash in wheelbarrows, and some burned banknotes to keep warm.
In 2009, Zimbabwe printed a one hundred trillion dollar note, and it was soon almost worthless.
So printing money forever doesn't make everyone rich. It makes everyone a billionaire who can't afford bread.

texte:
Your savings account is a turtle racing against inflation.

The Livret A is safe, simple and tax free. But when inflation runs faster than its rate, your balance goes up and your shopping cart still shrinks.

Great for emergencies. Follow for the rest of the race.

#livretA #epargne #personalfinance
script: What if your savings account was a turtle, racing against inflation?
In France, millions of people keep their savings in a Livret A. Safe, simple, tax free.
Right now, it pays one point seven percent a year.
Sounds fine. The turtle is moving.
But inflation is a hare, and lately it's been running at around three percent.
So every year, your turtle moves forward, but the finish line runs away even faster.
On paper, your balance goes up. At the supermarket, it buys a little less.
The turtle isn't losing because it's slow. It's losing because the race keeps moving.
Great for emergencies. Just don't expect the turtle to win the race.

texte:
Compound interest is a snowball. The secret isn't a bigger push.

1,000 euros at 7% a year doubles in about ten years, then again, then again. After 40 years: around 15,000 euros without adding a cent.

It's a longer mountain. Save this.

#compoundinterest #investing #longterm
script: What if compound interest was a snowball rolling down a mountain?
At the top, you push a tiny ball of snow. Say, a thousand euros.
At first, it barely grows. It picks up a little snow each year.
But here's the trick: the new snow sticks, and starts collecting snow of its own.
At seven percent a year, your thousand euros doubles in about ten years.
Then it doubles again. And again.
After forty years, it's around fifteen thousand euros, without adding a single cent.
The secret isn't a bigger push. It's a longer mountain.

texte:
Your crypto uncle has a new tip every Christmas. Ask him about last year's.

That's survivorship bias: you hear about the coin that tripled, never the five that went to zero.

Tag the uncle. You know the one.

#crypto #survivorshipbias #personalfinance
script: Why does your crypto expert uncle always have a new tip at Christmas dinner?
Every year, he's found the next big coin. And this time, it's going to the moon.
But have you noticed? He never talks about last year's coin.
That's survivorship bias. We hear about the winners, never about the ones that disappeared.
Thousands of crypto coins have been launched, and a huge number are now worth basically nothing.
Your uncle remembers the one coin that tripled.
He forgets the five that went to zero.
So his track record looks amazing. Well, the part he tells you.
Next Christmas, just ask him one question: how's last year's tip doing?

texte:
Could a bank safe survive a fall from 100 metres?

Some safes are drop-tested from about nine metres. A hundred is eleven times higher. The door might not make it. The money would.

Follow for more "what if" money questions.

#whatif #money #funfacts
script: Could a bank safe survive a fall from a hundred metres?
Safes are built to stop thieves, drills, and even fire.
Some fire-rated safes are even dropped from about nine metres during testing.
But a hundred metres is eleven times higher.
The safe would hit the ground at around a hundred and sixty kilometres an hour.
The steel walls might hold, but the door hinges and locking bolts take the shock.
The door could buckle, and the bolts could shear right off.
And inside? The money is fine. Paper doesn't break.
So the safe might not survive the fall. But your savings would.

texte:
One euro a day from the day you were born. How much at 65?

In a jar: about 24,000 euros. Invested at 7% a year: over 400,000. Time did the rest. (Illustrative: markets don't go up in a straight line.)

The best time to start was the day you were born. The second best is today.

#compoundinterest #investing #savings
script: What if your parents had saved just one euro a day, from the day you were born?
One euro. Less than a coffee.
On your eighteenth birthday, that's about six and a half thousand euros in a jar.
Nice. But a jar doesn't grow.
Now imagine it was invested at seven percent a year instead.
At eighteen, you'd have around twelve thousand euros.
At thirty, around thirty four thousand.
And at sixty five, over four hundred thousand euros. From one euro a day.
Only about twenty four thousand of that came out of anyone's pocket. Time did the rest.
So the best time to start was the day you were born. The second best is today.

texte:
Hidden fees are mosquitoes. One bite, you barely feel it.

10,000 euros at 6% for 20 years: about 32,000. With 3% a year in fees: about 18,000. That's 14,000 euros of blood, gone.

Read the label before you invest. Save this.

#fees #investing #personalfinance
script: What if hidden fees were mosquitoes, biting your money?
One bite? You barely feel it.
A management fee here. An entry fee there. A custody fee every single year.
Each one looks tiny. Half a percent. One percent.
But mosquitoes never come alone.
Stack up three percent a year in fees, and the bites start to add up.
Ten thousand euros growing at six percent for twenty years becomes about thirty two thousand.
With three percent in fees, it's only about eighteen thousand.
That's fourteen thousand euros of blood, gone.
So read the label before you invest. Or bring bug spray.

texte:
Where does one euro really go when you put it in an investment fund?

Entry fee, management fee, trading costs, custody fee. What's left finally reaches real companies, and they don't care how many people took a cut on the way.

The shortest road is often the cheapest. Follow for more.

#investing #fees #funds
script: Where does one euro really go when you put it into an investment fund?
You hand it over, and it starts its journey.
First stop, the advisor. Sometimes an entry fee takes a bite right away.
Next, the fund manager, with a management fee every single year.
Then trading costs, each time the fund buys and sells.
And the platform that holds it charges its own custody fee.
What's left finally gets invested in real companies.
But those companies don't care how many people took a cut on the way.
Your euro earns the market return, minus every bite along the road.
So when it comes to investing, the shortest road is often the cheapest one.

texte:
The dot com bubble, as an actual bubble floating over Wall Street.

The Nasdaq grew about five times in five years, then lost almost 80%. Even Amazon's stock fell more than 90%. Amazon survived. The bubble didn't.

Save this for the next "this time is different."

#stockmarket #bubble #moneyhistory
script: What if the dot com bubble was a real bubble, floating over Wall Street?
In the late nineties, anything with dot com in its name seemed to float up.
Investors kept blowing, and the Nasdaq grew about five times in five years.
In March 2000, it peaked above five thousand points.
Then: pop.
Over the next two and a half years, the Nasdaq lost almost eighty percent.
Pets dot com went from its stock market debut to shutting down in less than a year.
Even Amazon's stock fell more than ninety percent.
But Amazon survived. The bubble was fake. Some of the companies weren't.
Still, it took the Nasdaq fifteen years to get back to its old peak.

texte:
What if everyone took their money out of the bank on the same day?

Banks lend most deposits out. In 2023, customers pulled about 42 billion dollars from Silicon Valley Bank in one day. It collapsed the next morning.

In Europe, deposits are guaranteed up to 100,000 euros per person, per bank. Send this to someone who keeps everything in one bank.

#banking #bankrun #personalfinance
script: What if everyone took their money out of the bank on the same day?
Most people think their cash is sitting in a vault, waiting for them.
But banks lend most of it out: mortgages, business loans, car loans.
In the eurozone, banks only have to keep one percent of deposits as reserves at the central bank.
So if everyone shows up at once, there simply isn't enough cash.
That's a bank run. In 2023, customers pulled about forty two billion dollars from Silicon Valley Bank in a single day.
It collapsed the next morning.
That's why deposits in Europe are guaranteed up to one hundred thousand euros, per person, per bank.
So a bank's real superpower isn't the vault. It's everyone not panicking at the same time.

texte:
How many one cent coins does it take to sink a boat?

About 130,000. Roughly 1,300 euros of "basically nothing." Small amounts look harmless, until they add up.

Follow for one money idea a day.

#money #whatif #savings
script: How many one cent coins would it take to sink a boat?
One cent weighs just two point three grams.
Basically nothing. You could throw a handful in and never notice.
But a small rowboat can only carry about three hundred kilos.
That's around one hundred and thirty thousand coins.
Pour them in, and the boat sits lower, and lower.
Then water starts spilling over the edge, and down it goes.
All that for about thirteen hundred euros.
Small amounts look harmless. Until they add up.

texte:
Five ETFs doesn't mean you're diversified. Open the boxes.

World, US, tech, S&P 500, Nasdaq: the same ten giants weigh a quarter to half of each one. Five baskets, one basket, carried five times.

Check what's inside yours. Save this.

#ETF #diversification #investing
script: Why doesn't owning five different ETFs make you diversified?
You buy a world fund, a US fund, a tech fund, an S and P five hundred fund, and a Nasdaq fund.
Five names. Five tickers. You feel very safe.
But open the boxes, and look inside.
In a world index, the ten biggest companies already weigh about a quarter.
In the S and P five hundred, around a third. In the Nasdaq hundred, close to half.
And they're the same ten giants, again and again.
So your five baskets are really one big basket, carried five times.
If those giants stumble, all five funds fall together.
Diversifying isn't owning more funds. It's owning different things.

texte:
Your savings are asleep. And they're snoring.

Most current accounts pay exactly zero while prices keep rising. Keep enough awake for emergencies, put the rest to work.

Money that sleeps too long wakes up poorer. Follow for more.

#savings #inflation #personalfinance
script: What if your savings were literally asleep?
Money sitting in a current account earns, at most banks, exactly zero.
It's not lazy. It's just snoring.
Meanwhile, prices keep rising, so every year, the same pile buys a little less.
In France, households keep hundreds of billions of euros sleeping in current accounts.
But waking it up doesn't mean taking crazy risks.
Even a regulated savings account pays something, and your money stays available.
Keep enough awake for emergencies, and put the rest to work.
Because money that sleeps too long wakes up poorer.

texte:
In 1976, one man owned 10% of Apple. He sold it for 800 dollars.

Ronald Wayne drew Apple's first logo, then quit 12 days in, scared of paying the company's debts himself. A year later he took 1,500 more to drop any claim. On paper, that 10% would be worth hundreds of billions today.

He says he doesn't regret it. Send this to someone who sold too early.

#apple #moneyhistory #investing
script: In 1976, one man owned ten percent of Apple.
His name was Ronald Wayne.
He wrote the contract, drew the very first logo, and was twice as old as Steve Jobs.
But Wayne was nervous.
In a partnership, every partner pays the company's debts out of his own pocket.
And Jobs had just bought fifteen thousand dollars of parts on credit.
Wayne had just finished paying off a failed business.
So twelve days after Apple was born, he quit and sold his share for eight hundred dollars.
A year later, he took fifteen hundred more to give up any claim.
Today, ten percent of Apple would be worth, on paper, hundreds of billions of dollars.
And Wayne says he doesn't regret it.
Otherwise, he joked, he would just be the richest man in the cemetery.

texte:
In 2013, a man in Wales threw away a hard drive. On it: 8,000 bitcoins.

It went out with the trash by mistake, straight to the landfill. Today those coins are worth hundreds of millions of dollars, buried under tons of garbage. The city said no to digging, and a judge threw out his case.

After more than a decade, he gave up. Send this to someone who never backs anything up.

#bitcoin #crypto #moneyhistory
script: In 2013, a man in Wales threw away a hard drive.
On it were eight thousand bitcoins.
He says it went out with the trash by mistake, straight to the local landfill.
Back then, bitcoin was cheap.
But the price exploded.
Today, those coins are worth hundreds of millions of dollars, buried under tons of garbage.
He offered the city a share of the fortune if they let him dig.
The city said no, and a judge threw out his case.
After more than a decade, he finally gave up.
So somewhere under Newport lies one of the most expensive pieces of trash on Earth.

texte:
A secretary bought 3 shares for 180 dollars in the 1930s. She never sold them.

Grace Groner lived in a one-bedroom house and bought her clothes secondhand. She reinvested every dividend. When she died in 2010, at 100, her shares were worth about 7 million dollars.

She left almost all of it to her old college. Save this for the day you feel like selling too early.

#investing #dividends #moneyhistory
script: In the 1930s, a secretary bought three shares of the company she worked for.
Sixty dollars each, a hundred and eighty in total.
Her name was Grace Groner, and she never sold them.
She lived in a tiny one-bedroom house, bought her clothes secondhand, and walked everywhere.
Everyone thought she had almost nothing.
But her three shares kept quietly multiplying.
The company split its stock again and again, and she reinvested every dividend.
Three shares became more than a hundred thousand.
When she died in 2010, at a hundred years old, they were worth about seven million dollars.
And she left almost all of it to her old college, to pay for students' studies and travels.
Not bad for a hundred and eighty dollars.

texte:
One forgotten server. 45 minutes. More than 400 million dollars gone.

In 2012, Knight Capital copied new software onto eight servers. A technician forgot one. Old code woke up and started buying high and selling low: over 4 million trades.

The firm had to be rescued within days. Follow for more money stories.

#stockmarket #wallstreet #moneyhistory
script: On August first, 2012, a trading firm switched on new software.
Knight Capital handled a huge share of all American stock trades.
The update had to be copied onto eight servers.
But a technician forgot one.
On that forgotten server, an old piece of code woke up.
It started buying high and selling low, again and again, thousands of times per second.
In forty-five minutes, it made over four million trades.
Nobody could find the off switch fast enough.
When it finally stopped, Knight had lost more than four hundred million dollars.
Its stock collapsed, and the firm had to be rescued within days.
All because of one server that missed an update.

texte:
He pumped gas for 25 years, then worked as a janitor. He left almost 8 million dollars.

Ronald Read drove a used car and held his coat together with safety pins. His secret was boring: shares in big, solid companies, dividends reinvested, almost never sold.

He left most of it to the local hospital and library. Send this to someone who thinks boring can't win.

#investing #dividends #moneyhistory
script: In a small town in Vermont, a man pumped gas for twenty-five years.
Then he worked as a janitor.
His name was Ronald Read.
He drove a used car, chopped his own firewood, and held his coat together with safety pins.
Nobody thought he had any money.
But when he died in 2014, at ninety-two, his town was stunned.
Ronald had left behind almost eight million dollars.
His secret was boring.
For decades, he bought shares in big, solid companies he understood.
He reinvested the dividends, and he almost never sold.
His stock certificates filled a safe deposit box five inches thick.
And he left most of it to the local hospital and library.
Not bad for a janitor.

texte:
On April 20, 2020, the price of oil went below zero.

A barrel of American oil closed at minus 37 dollars. Sellers were paying people to take it. Lockdown, storage tanks filling up fast, and contracts ending the next day: receive real barrels, or pay someone to take them.

For one day, oil was worth less than nothing. Follow for more money stories.

#oil #stockmarket #moneyhistory
script: On April twentieth, 2020, the price of oil did something impossible.
It went below zero.
A barrel of American oil closed at minus thirty-seven dollars.
That means sellers were paying people to take their oil.
The world was in lockdown, so planes were grounded and cars stayed home.
But the oil kept coming out of the ground.
Storage tanks were filling up fast.
And many traders held contracts that ended the next day.
If they didn't sell, they would have to receive real barrels of oil, with nowhere to put them.
So they paid anyone who would take them.
For one day, oil was literally worth less than nothing.

texte:
Isaac Newton figured out gravity. Then he lost a fortune in a bubble.

In 1720 he bought South Sea Company shares, sold early with a nice profit, then watched the price climb from about 100 pounds to nearly 1,000. He jumped back in with much more money. The bubble burst, and he reportedly lost around 20,000 pounds.

Even a genius can catch the fear of missing out. Send this to a friend who chases every hype.

#investing #fomo #moneyhistory
script: Isaac Newton was one of the smartest people who ever lived.
Gravity, light, calculus, all him.
In 1720, everyone in London was buying shares of the South Sea Company.
Newton bought some too, then sold early, with a nice profit.
Smart move.
But the price kept climbing, from about a hundred pounds to nearly a thousand.
His friends were getting rich, and Newton couldn't stand it.
So he jumped back in, at a much higher price, with much more money.
A few months later, the bubble burst, and the shares crashed.
Newton reportedly lost around twenty thousand pounds, a fortune at the time.
He is said to have joked that he could calculate the motion of the stars, but not the madness of people.
Even a genius can catch the fear of missing out.
On May sixth, 2010, at about two forty in the afternoon, Wall Street fell off a cliff.
In just a few minutes, the Dow dropped almost a thousand points.
Nearly a trillion dollars vanished from the market.
Some shares of huge companies traded for one cent.
But then, almost as fast, it all came back.
Within about twenty minutes, most of the losses were gone.
Investigators blamed a giant automatic sell order.
Trading computers reacted to each other in milliseconds, dumping shares in a panic loop.
Years later, a British trader working from his parents' home was also charged for helping trigger it.
So for a few minutes, the world's biggest market went crazy, and then acted like nothing happened.
In the 1630s, in Holland, people went crazy over tulips.
The rarest ones had wild, flame-like stripes.
Nobody knew it then, but those stripes were caused by a virus.
Prices exploded.
A single rare bulb reportedly cost as much as a fine house in Amsterdam.
Others sold for several years of a craftsman's salary.
But here's the funny part: most of the trading happened in taverns, on paper, in winter.
People were buying and selling bulbs that were still in the ground.
Then, in February 1637, at an auction, nobody showed up to buy.
Within days, prices collapsed.
Historians think the drama was exaggerated later, but the lesson stuck.
When something is only worth what the next person will pay, one empty room can end it all.
In 2009, Zimbabwe printed a banknote worth one hundred trillion dollars.
That's a one with fourteen zeros.
And it still couldn't buy much.
Back in 2008, prices were rising so fast they doubled roughly every day.
At the peak, monthly inflation was estimated in the billions of percent.
But how does money lose value that fast?
The government printed more and more money to pay its bills, while the economy was shrinking.
More money chasing fewer goods means every note buys less.
Shops changed prices several times a day, and people carried bricks of cash.
The country cut zeros off its money again and again.
In the end, Zimbabwe gave up its own currency and used foreign ones, like the US dollar.
Today, those hundred trillion dollar notes are sold online as souvenirs.
In December 2005, a trader in Tokyo wanted to sell one share for six hundred and ten thousand yen.
Instead, he sold six hundred and ten thousand shares, for one yen each.
He had swapped the two numbers.
The company, J-Com, only had about fourteen thousand shares in total.
So he was selling more than forty times the whole company.
A warning popped up on his screen, and he ignored it.
But when his firm, Mizuho, tried to cancel, the exchange's system failed.
The order went through.
Traders all over Japan snapped up the bargain shares.
Mizuho lost about forty billion yen, hundreds of millions of dollars.
It later sued the stock exchange, and won part of the money back.
All because of one typo.
In 1923, in Germany, a loaf of bread cost about two hundred billion marks.
At the start of that same year, it cost a few hundred.
Prices were rising by the hour.
Workers were paid twice a day, and ran to the shops before their money lost its value.
People pushed their wages home in wheelbarrows.
A famous joke says a thief stole the wheelbarrow, and left the cash on the ground.
But the strangest part was what people did with the notes.
Children built towers and kites with them.
Some burned money in the stove, because it was cheaper than buying wood.
Others used it as wallpaper.
By November, one US dollar was worth over four trillion marks.
Germany finally replaced the old money with a new currency: one new mark for a trillion old ones.
In April 2018, an employee at Samsung Securities had one simple job.
Pay a dividend of one thousand won per share to staff who owned company stock.
Instead, he typed one thousand shares.
Per share.
In seconds, the firm created about two point eight billion shares out of thin air.
That's more than thirty times all the real shares that existed.
On paper, they were worth over a hundred billion dollars.
But here's the wild part: some employees started selling them.
Within about half an hour, around five million ghost shares were dumped on the market.
The stock dropped sharply before trading was stopped.
Several employees were later convicted, and the CEO resigned.
One wrong unit, a hundred billion dollars of fake money.
Barings was Britain's oldest merchant bank, more than two hundred years old.
It even helped America buy Louisiana.
In 1995, one single trader brought it down.
His name was Nick Leeson, and he worked in Singapore.
He bet huge sums on the Japanese stock market.
When he lost, he hid the losses in a secret account, numbered eight eight eight eight eight.
Then he bet even bigger, to win it all back.
But in January 1995, an earthquake hit Kobe, and Japanese stocks crashed.
His losses reached eight hundred and twenty-seven million pounds, roughly twice the bank's capital.
Leeson fled, leaving a note that said: I'm sorry.
Barings collapsed, and was sold for one pound.
Two centuries of history, ended by one secret account.
In August 2020, Citibank had to send a small interest payment for the cosmetics company Revlon.
About eight million dollars.
Instead, it sent nine hundred million.
The problem was the software.
To avoid sending the whole loan, an employee had to tick three boxes.
He ticked one.
And two other people approved it.
Some lenders gave the money back.
But others, holding about half a billion dollars, said: thanks, we're keeping it.
Citibank sued, and in 2021, a judge actually agreed with the lenders.
But in 2022, an appeals court reversed it, and Citi finally got its money back.
Two unchecked boxes, two years in court.
On Monday, October nineteenth, 1987, the US stock market lost almost a quarter of its value.
In a single day.
The Dow fell twenty-two point six percent.
It's still the biggest one-day drop in its history.
Panic had started in Asia and Europe, and hit New York at the opening bell.
But the real twist was a strategy called portfolio insurance.
Computers were set to sell automatically when prices fell.
Selling made prices fall, which triggered even more selling.
Phones rang nonstop, and the price ticker ran more than an hour behind.
Afterwards, exchanges added circuit breakers, automatic pauses when markets fall too fast.
And the Dow won back its losses in about two years.
In 2011, a programmer named Stefan Thomas was paid for making a video about bitcoin.
He got seven thousand and two bitcoins.
Back then, they weren't worth much.
He stored the keys on a special encrypted USB drive.
And wrote the password on a piece of paper.
Then he lost the paper.
But here's the cruel part: the drive gives you ten tries.
After the tenth wrong password, it erases itself forever.
He has already used eight.
Two guesses left, for coins now worth hundreds of millions of dollars.
Hackers have offered to crack it, but as far as we know, the coins are still locked.
Maybe the most expensive password ever forgotten.
For three years, Switzerland promised one thing.
One euro would never be worth less than one franc twenty.
Traders treated it like a wall.
Just days before, a central bank official called it a cornerstone of its policy.
But on January fifteenth, 2015, at ten thirty in the morning, the wall vanished.
With no warning, the Swiss National Bank dropped the floor.
Within minutes, the franc jumped about thirty percent at its peak.
Traders betting against the franc were wiped out, and many couldn't cover their losses.
The broker Alpari UK went bankrupt.
The giant FXCM lost around two hundred and twenty-five million dollars and needed an emergency loan.
The safest bet in finance broke in one morning.
In January 2021, a struggling video game store became the hottest stock on Earth.
Big hedge funds were betting GameStop would fall.
In total, they had shorted more shares than were actually available to trade.
But on Reddit, a forum called WallStreetBets noticed.
Huge numbers of small investors started buying, together.
When a short bet goes wrong, the fund has to buy shares back to close it.
That buying pushes the price even higher, which forces more buying.

GameStop went from under twenty dollars to over four hundred, in a few weeks.
One hedge fund, Melvin Capital, lost more than half its money and needed a multibillion dollar rescue.
Then some trading apps restricted buying, and the price came crashing back down.

Worth more than the oil giant ExxonMobil.
Many hedge funds had bet that VW's stock would fall.
But on a Sunday, Porsche revealed it controlled about seventy-four percent of Volkswagen.
A German state owned another twenty percent.
That left only around six percent of the shares free to trade.
The problem: short sellers needed to buy back far more than that.
Everyone rushed for the same tiny pile of shares.
In two days, the stock jumped from around two hundred euros to over a thousand.

What if you could buy five hundred companies with one click?
That's what an ETF can do.
It stands for exchange-traded fund.
Think of it like a fruit basket.
Instead of picking one apple and hoping it's not rotten, you buy the whole basket.
Many ETFs simply copy an index, like the five hundred biggest American companies.
When one company stumbles, the others soften the fall.
And it trades on the stock market, just like a single share.
But not every basket is the same.
Some hold only one sector, some charge higher fees, some use complex tricks.
So before you buy the basket, look at what's inside.

In finance, leverage works the same way.
You put in a little money, and borrow the rest.
With a hundred dollars of yours and nine hundred borrowed, you control a thousand.
If the price rises ten percent, you make a hundred dollars.
You just doubled your money.
But the lever works both ways.
If the price falls ten percent, you lose a hundred dollars.
Your money is gone, and you still owe the loan.
Fall a little more, and you lose more than you ever put in.
That's why leverage is called a double-edged sword.
In 2008, Warren Buffett made a bet worth a million dollars.
His claim: a boring, cheap index fund would beat top hedge fund managers over ten years.
One money manager, Ted Seides, accepted.
He picked five funds, each investing in many hedge funds run by professionals.
Buffett simply picked a fund that copied the five hundred biggest American companies.
Then the financial crisis hit, and the hedge funds started ahead.
But year after year, the index caught up, then pulled away.
The big reason: fees.
Hedge funds often charged around two percent a year, plus a share of the profits.
After ten years, the index fund was up about one hundred and twenty-six percent.
The hedge fund picks: about thirty-six percent, on average.
Buffett won, and the money went to a charity for girls in Omaha.
In 2000, Enron was one of the hottest companies in America.
A business magazine called it America's most innovative company, six years in a row.
Its stock hit around ninety dollars.

And it hid billions in debt inside side companies, off its books.

The stock fell below one dollar, and Enron went bankrupt.
Thousands of employees lost their jobs, and many lost retirement savings held in Enron stock.
Its famous auditor collapsed too.
And America passed new laws to make companies prove their numbers.
Everyone wants to buy at the bottom.
But nobody knows where the bottom is.

It's called dollar-cost averaging.
Say you put in one hundred dollars each month.
Month one, the price is ten dollars: you get ten shares.
Month two, it crashes to five: your hundred buys twenty shares.
Month three, back to ten: ten more shares.
You spent three hundred dollars for forty shares.
That's seven fifty per share, cheaper than the average price.
When prices fall, your money automatically buys more.
It doesn't promise profits, but it removes the guessing.
Which company is bigger: one whose share costs a thousand dollars, or one whose share costs ten?
Most people pick the thousand dollar one.
But the share price alone tells you almost nothing.
What matters is market capitalization.
It's simple: the share price, times the number of shares.
Company A: a thousand dollars a share, but only one million shares. That's one billion.
Company B: ten dollars a share, but one billion shares. That's ten billion.
The cheap share belongs to the company that's ten times bigger.
Market cap is what the whole company is worth on the stock market.
It's how investors compare giants, and how many indexes choose their members.
In 1920, a man in Boston promised you fifty percent profit in just forty-five days.
His name was Charles Ponzi.
His idea sounded clever: international postal reply coupons.
You could buy them cheaply in some countries, and trade them for more valuable stamps in America.
But to make real money, he would have needed millions of coupons, far more than existed.
So he barely bought any.
Instead, he paid early investors with the money from new investors.
Those happy investors told their friends, and the money poured in.
Within months, he had collected millions of dollars.
Then a newspaper started asking questions, and the new money stopped.
Without new money, the whole thing collapsed.
Today, any scheme that pays old investors with new money carries his name: a Ponzi scheme.
In the late seventies, two Texas oil billionaires tried to corner the world's silver.
The Hunt brothers bought silver bars and silver contracts, again and again.
They ended up controlling a huge share of the world's tradeable silver.
The price went from about six dollars an ounce to around fifty.
People lined up to melt down their grandmothers' silverware.
But the exchange changed the rules, and limited buying with borrowed money.
The brothers had bought much of their silver with loans.
When the price started falling, their lenders demanded more cash.
On March twenty-seventh, 1980, silver crashed to around ten dollars.
They called it Silver Thursday.
Banks had to arrange a billion dollar rescue, to stop the panic from spreading.
Years later, the Hunt brothers went bankrupt.
Why do traders talk about bulls and bears?
A bull market means prices are rising.
A bear market means prices are falling.
The popular explanation: a bull attacks by thrusting its horns upward.
A bear attacks by swiping its paws downward.
But the real story may be older, and stranger.
In eighteenth century London, there was a saying: don't sell the bear's skin before you've caught the bear.
Traders who sold shares they didn't own yet, hoping prices would drop, were called bearskin jobbers, then simply bears.
Bulls probably came along as their natural opponents.
Today, a drop of twenty percent from a peak is often called a bear market.
And in New York, a bronze bull still charges near Wall Street.
Ever exchanged money at an airport?
The booth buys euros at one price, and sells them at a higher one.
That gap is called the spread.
On the stock market, every share has two prices too.
The bid: the highest price someone will pay.
The ask: the lowest price someone will sell for.
If you buy and then sell instantly, you lose the difference.
For huge companies traded all day, the spread is usually tiny, often just a cent.
But for small or rarely traded stocks, it can be wide.
It's a hidden cost that never shows up as a fee.
So before you click buy, check the gap.
Bernie Madoff was a Wall Street legend.
He had even been chairman of the Nasdaq stock market.
His fund promised something magical: steady gains of about ten percent a year, whether markets went up or down.
Investors begged to get in.
But the returns were too smooth to be true.
A financial analyst named Harry Markopolos warned regulators for years.
They didn't stop it.
Behind the scenes, Madoff simply paid old clients with new clients' money.
In 2008, the financial crisis hit, and investors asked for billions back.
The money wasn't there.
Madoff confessed. His statements showed about sixty-five billion dollars that didn't exist.
He was sentenced to a hundred and fifty years in prison.
In 1994, a hedge fund launched with an all-star team.
Top Wall Street traders, and two economists who would soon win the Nobel Prize.
It was called Long-Term Capital Management.
Their computer models hunted tiny price differences between similar bonds.
Each bet earned very little, so they borrowed heavily to make it big.
At times, they had about twenty-five dollars of bets for every dollar of their own.
For a few years, it worked brilliantly: around forty percent a year.
But in 1998, Russia defaulted on its debt.
Panicked investors fled to the safest assets, and the price gaps grew instead of closing.
Borrowing turned small losses into giant ones: more than four billion dollars in a few months.
Fearing a chain reaction, the New York Fed brought banks together to rescue the fund.
Genius models, undone by too much borrowing.
What if a company paid you just for owning a piece of it?
That's a dividend.
When a company makes a profit, it has two choices.
Keep the money to grow, or share some of it with its shareholders.
Say a company pays two dollars per share each year, and you own fifty shares.
That's a hundred dollars in your pocket, without selling anything.
But dividends are never guaranteed.
In bad years, companies can cut them, or stop them completely.
And on payment day, the share price usually drops by about the same amount.
The money just moved from the company to you.
Many investors reinvest their dividends to buy more shares, which then pay more dividends.
Slowly, the snowball grows.
In 1973, an economist claimed a blindfolded monkey throwing darts could pick stocks as well as the experts.
The Wall Street Journal decided to test it.
From 1988, its staff threw darts at the stock pages.
Whatever the darts hit, they picked.
At the same time, professional investors picked their best ideas.
Six months later, they compared the results.
The contest ran for about fourteen years, and more than a hundred rounds.
So who won? The pros, more often.
But not by a landslide: the darts still won roughly four rounds out of ten.
And critics noted the pros' picks got a boost just from being published in the paper.
Paying a lot for expert picks? Make sure they beat a dart.
You own a house worth three hundred thousand dollars, and you need cash tomorrow.
Good luck.
Selling a house can take months: visits, paperwork, negotiations.
And if you're in a hurry, you might have to drop the price.
Now imagine you own three hundred thousand dollars of a big company's shares.
You click sell, and it's done in seconds, at a price close to the last one.
That difference has a name: liquidity.
It's how quickly you can turn something into cash, without losing value.
Cash itself is the most liquid thing there is.
Houses, art, or shares of a tiny company are much less liquid.
But liquidity can vanish in a panic, when everyone wants to sell at once.
So always keep some cash for emergencies.
Lehman Brothers had survived for over a hundred and fifty years.
Wars, crashes, the Great Depression.
But by 2008, it had bet heavily on American home loans, with lots of borrowed money.
When house prices fell, those bets turned toxic.
On Friday, September twelfth, top bankers were called to the New York Fed.
All weekend, they searched for a buyer.
Bank of America walked away. A British bank's deal fell through.
And the government refused to bail it out.
On Monday morning, Lehman filed for bankruptcy, the biggest in American history.
Employees walked out carrying their things in cardboard boxes.
Markets crashed, and panic spread around the world.
A hundred and fifty years, gone in one weekend.
Does Santa Claus visit Wall Street?
Some traders think he does.
In 1972, Yale Hirsch spotted a pattern in his stock market almanac.
In the last five trading days of December and the first two of January, stocks tend to rise.
He called it the Santa Claus rally.
Since 1950, the American market has gone up in that window roughly three times out of four, by about one percent on average.
Why? Nobody knows for sure.
Holiday cheer, year-end bonuses, and quiet markets while many traders are on vacation.
But it's a tendency, not a promise.
Some years, Santa never shows up.
Hirsch even warned that when Santa skips Wall Street, the bears might come next.
So enjoy the rally, but don't build your plan on it.
How much would the Twelve Days of Christmas really cost?
A bank actually calculates it, every year since 1984.
It's called the PNC Christmas Price Index.
A partridge in a pear tree, two turtle doves, all the way to twelve drummers drumming.
In 2025, one set of all those gifts cost over fifty-one thousand dollars.
Up four and a half percent in a single year.
But in the song, the gifts repeat every day.
That's three hundred and sixty-four gifts in total.
Buy them all, and the bill passes two hundred thousand dollars.
The fun part: it works like a tiny inflation index.
The dancers, pipers and drummers follow wages, while the birds follow food and pet prices.
So next time someone sings it, you'll know the price of love.
Every Christmas, one economist sees billions of dollars disappear.
In 1993, Joel Waldfogel asked students a simple question about their gifts.
How much did it cost? And how much would you have paid for it yourself?
The answers didn't match.
On average, people valued their gifts somewhere between ten and thirty-three percent less than their price.
He called it the deadweight loss of Christmas.
Picture a fifty dollar sweater that you would only pay thirty dollars for.
Twenty dollars of value just vanished.
Gifts from distant relatives lost the most. Close friends and partners did better.
And cash? No loss at all, but it can feel a bit cold.
Of course, economics can't measure the feeling of being thought of.
So give smart: ask, listen, or make it personal.
Rudolph the red-nosed reindeer wasn't born in a legend.
He was born in a marketing department.
In 1939, the Chicago store Montgomery Ward wanted a free Christmas booklet to bring families into its shops.
A copywriter named Robert May got the job.
He wrote about a misfit reindeer, mocked for his glowing nose, who ends up guiding Santa's sleigh.
That first year, the store gave away about two point four million copies.
But here's the twist: the story belonged to the company, not to May.
And May was deep in debt from his late wife's medical bills.
In 1947, the company's boss handed him the rights.
Two years later, May's brother-in-law turned it into a song.
It became one of the best-selling Christmas songs ever, and May finally got rich.
A free ad became a Christmas classic.
Many people think Coca-Cola invented Santa's red suit.
It didn't.
Red-suited Santas already showed up in magazines and ads decades earlier.
But Coca-Cola did something powerful with him.
In the early 1930s, the company had a problem: people drank fewer cold sodas in winter.
So in 1931, it hired the artist Haddon Sundblom to paint Santa for its Christmas ads.
His Santa was warm, chubby and jolly, with rosy cheeks and a big white beard.
And he was often holding a bottle of Coke.
Sundblom kept painting him for more than thirty years.
Those ads ran everywhere, year after year.
So Coca-Cola didn't invent Santa, but its ads helped lock in the image most of us picture today.
That's the power of repetition in marketing.
Imagine a savings account that paid you almost nothing and locked your money away for a whole year.
Sounds terrible, right?
Yet millions of Americans signed up for one.
It was called a Christmas Club.
The idea is usually traced back to a bank in Pennsylvania around 1909.
You put in a small fixed amount every week, like one dollar.
You couldn't touch it until late November.
And the interest was tiny, sometimes zero.
But that was the point.
People knew that money sitting in their pocket would disappear.
The club removed the temptation.
Economists call this a commitment device: you tie your own hands today to help your future self.
So when December came, the gift money was already there.
Sometimes the best financial tool is the one that stops you from spending.
Every Christmas, millions of people get a gift card.
And a lot of them never get spent.
Surveys suggest nearly half of American adults have at least one unused gift card, worth billions of dollars in total.
The card gets lost in a drawer.
Or there are five dollars left, too little to bother.
Or the store closes before you use it.
For the shop, this is great news.
It already has your money.
The unspent part even has a name: breakage.
Companies estimate how much will never be used and count it as revenue.
So a gift card is cash that slowly forgets it exists.
If you get one this Christmas, spend it in January, before it becomes a gift to the store.
For many stores, the whole year is decided in just two months.
In the US, November and December bring in roughly a fifth of all retail sales for the year.
For toy shops, it can be even more.
That's why the day after Thanksgiving is called Black Friday.
You've probably heard the story: it's the day stores stop losing money, in the red, and start making money, in the black.
Nice story.
But the name most likely came from Philadelphia police in the 1960s.
They hated that day: huge crowds, traffic jams, total chaos.
Stores later preferred the profit version, and it stuck.
Either way, the lesson is real.
When a business depends on one season, a bad December can ruin the whole year.
So next time a shop screams last chance, remember who really needs that sale.
The Christmas tree in your living room is probably older than you think.
A typical farm tree takes around seven to ten years to grow to about two meters.
The farmer plants a tiny seedling, and waits.
Year one: almost nothing.
Year three: still small.
No harvest, no money, just watering, trimming and protecting it.
Then, after years of patience, it finally becomes a full tree worth selling.
Investing works a bit like that.
At first, your money barely seems to grow.
Many people quit right there.
But growth builds on growth, and the later years do most of the work.
So if you want a tree for Christmas in ten years, the best time to plant it is today.
This Christmas, a kid gets a one hundred dollar toy.
By February, it's under the bed.
Now imagine the same hundred dollars put into a simple index fund instead.
If it grew around seven percent a year, which is never guaranteed, by age eighteen it could be worth about three hundred and forty dollars.
Do that every Christmas, and eighteen gifts of one hundred dollars could grow to around three thousand six hundred.
That's double what you put in.
The secret isn't the amount.
It's time.
A child has the one thing most adults wish they had more of: decades ahead.
You don't have to skip the toy.
But one small gift can keep growing long after the wrapping paper is gone.
How long does it take to double your money?
There's a shortcut.
It's called the rule of seventy-two.
Take seventy-two and divide it by your yearly return.
At six percent a year, your money doubles in about twelve years.
At nine percent, about eight years.
At two percent, like a sleepy savings account, about thirty-six years.
It also works backwards.
If prices rise three percent a year, your money loses half its value in about twenty-four years.
And if a credit card charges twenty-four percent and you never pay, the debt doubles in about three years.
It's not perfectly exact, but it's close enough to do in your head.
Seventy-two: the tiny number that shows how fast money grows, or melts.
Your money is shrinking, even when the number stays the same.
That's inflation.
Imagine a sandwich costs five dollars today.
If prices rise three percent a year, in ten years the same sandwich costs about six dollars seventy.
Your five dollar bill didn't change.
But it buys less.
Why does it happen?
Often, when more money chases the same amount of stuff, prices go up.
A little inflation, around two percent, is actually what many central banks aim for.
Too much is a disaster: just ask Germany in 1923, or Zimbabwe in 2008.
So cash under the mattress isn't really safe.
It's slowly melting.
That's why people invest: not only to get rich, but to keep up.
Let's flip a coin.
Heads, you win one hundred and fifty dollars.
Tails, you lose one hundred.
On average, that's a good bet.
Yet most people say no.
That's loss aversion.
Psychologists Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky found that losing feels roughly twice as bad as winning the same amount feels good.
It explains a lot.
Why people panic and sell when the market drops.
Why they hold a losing stock forever, just hoping to get even.
And why so much cash sits in savings accounts instead of being invested.
Your brain is built to avoid pain, not to grow your money.
Knowing that is the first step to beating it.
During World War Two, the US military had a problem.
Too many bombers were being shot down.
So they studied the planes that came back, covered in bullet holes.
Most holes were on the wings and the body.
The obvious idea: add armor where the holes are.
But, as the famous story goes, a statistician named Abraham Wald said the opposite.
Put armor where there are no holes.
Why?
Because planes hit in those spots, like the engines, never made it back.
That's survivorship bias: you only see the winners.
It happens in finance all the time.
You hear about the guy who got rich on one coin, not the thousands who lost.
And funds that did badly often get closed, so the ones still around look better than average.
Before you copy a success story, ask: who didn't make it back?
Your car breaks down.
The repair costs eight hundred dollars.
Where does that money come from?
For many people, it goes on a credit card, at twenty percent interest or more.
Now a small problem has become a growing debt.

It's money set aside only for surprises: a broken phone, a medical bill, losing your job.
A common rule of thumb is three to six months of essential expenses.
Keep it somewhere safe and easy to reach, like a savings account, not in the stock market.
It won't make you rich.
Its job is different.
It turns a disaster into an inconvenience.
And it lets your investments keep growing, instead of selling them at the worst moment.
What is a bond?
Simple: it's a loan, but this time you're the bank.
A company or a government needs money.
So it borrows from you.
Say you lend one thousand dollars for five years.
Every year, they pay you interest, called the coupon, maybe forty dollars.
At the end of the five years, you get your thousand back.
That's why bonds are usually calmer than stocks.
But they're not risk free.
If the borrower goes bankrupt, you might not get all your money back.
And if interest rates rise, older bonds that pay less become less attractive, so their price drops.
Stocks make you an owner.
Bonds make you a lender.
Many investors hold both, to balance growth and calm.
In 1976, a man named John Bogle launched a strange fund.
It didn't try to pick winning stocks.
It simply bought the whole market, the five hundred biggest US companies, and kept costs tiny.
Wall Street laughed.
People called it Bogle's folly.
One poster even claimed index funds were un-American.
He hoped to raise about one hundred fifty million dollars.
He got around eleven million.
But his idea was simple: most professional managers fail to beat the market over time, especially after fees.
So why pay them?

Index funds now hold trillions of dollars, and that once mocked fund grew into one of the biggest in the world.
Sometimes the boring idea wins.

Because there really was a wall.
In the sixteen hundreds, New York was a small Dutch town called New Amsterdam.

The path running along it became known as Wall Street.
The British later tore the wall down, but the name stayed.

They signed a short agreement on how to trade with each other.
That deal is often seen as the birth of what became the New York Stock Exchange.
So the most famous financial street in the world is named after a wooden fence.
And it all started with two dozen guys under a tree.
Imagine paying for groceries with a sack of iron coins.
That was daily life in parts of China about a thousand years ago.
In Sichuan, coins were made of iron, so a simple purchase could weigh several kilos.
So merchants had an idea.
Leave your heavy coins with us, and we'll give you a paper receipt.
People started trading the receipts themselves.
They were called jiaozi.
Around 1023, the Song government took control and issued official paper money, one of the first in the world.
Centuries later, Marco Polo was amazed that people accepted paper as payment.

When rulers needed money, they printed more and more, and prices exploded.
Paper money was a brilliant invention.
And so was the temptation to print too much.

Ships could sink, get attacked, or never come back.
One voyage could make you rich, or wipe you out.

Instead of a few rich men funding one trip, ordinary people could buy a small piece of the whole company.
Maids, merchants, craftsmen: more than a thousand people bought in, in Amsterdam alone.
If one ship sank, the company kept going.
And if you needed your money, you could sell your share to someone else.
People traded these shares in Amsterdam, in one of the first stock exchanges.
Early on, some dividends were even paid in spices.
That's why the VOC is often called the first company to sell shares to the public.
Every share you own today carries a little bit of that Dutch idea.
What if missing just ten days could cut your money in half?
Put ten thousand dollars in the S&P 500 in 2004.
Leave it alone for twenty years: about sixty-three thousand.
But say a crash scares you, and you sell.
You miss only the ten best days, out of about five thousand.
You end with twenty-nine thousand. Less than half.
Miss twenty, and it's seventeen thousand.
The cruel part? Seven of the ten best days came within two weeks of the ten worst.
The big rebounds arrive right after the scary drops, while everyone is hiding.
Nobody rings a bell before the best day.
That's why time in the market usually beats timing the market.

Nice. So you upgrade the phone.
Then the car. Then a bigger apartment.
A few months later, the extra money is gone, and you're just as tight as before.

Two hundred fifty dollars a month, growing seven percent a year, for ten years.

And as the balance shrinks, the minimum shrinks too.
Keep paying only the minimum, and it takes about nineteen years to clear.

Done in under three years, with about seventeen hundred in interest.

What if a convicted killer once ran the money of an entire country?
John Law, a Scottish gambler, killed a man in a duel and escaped from prison.
In 1716 he lands in France, a country drowning in war debts.
His big idea: replace gold coins with paper money.
Then he sells shares in the Mississippi Company, promising riches from Louisiana.
The share price jumps from about five hundred livres to around ten thousand.
Servants get rich overnight. Legend says the word millionaire was born here.
But Louisiana is mostly swamp. The riches never come.
In 1720, everyone rushes to swap paper for coins. Prices collapse.
Law flees France and dies poor in Venice.

What if the real price of something isn't on the tag?
Say you buy a five dollar coffee every workday.
That's about twelve hundred dollars a year. Fine, it's coffee.
But economists ask a different question: what did you give up?
That's opportunity cost: the value of the best option you didn't choose.
Invest those twelve hundred dollars a year at seven percent instead.
After thirty years, you'd have more than a hundred thousand dollars.
So that coffee never really cost five dollars.
It works with time too. An hour scrolling is an hour not learning, sleeping, or seeing friends.
This doesn't mean never buy coffee.
It means every yes is also a no. Just make sure it's worth it.
What if one man spent so much gold that he crashed its price in an entire city?

He hands out gold to officials, merchants, and the poor.
Suddenly, Cairo is flooded with gold.
And when something becomes common, it's worth less.
According to a writer of the time, gold in Cairo was still worth less twelve years later.

Because money only works when it's scarce.
What if someone sold the Eiffel Tower, and got away with it?
Paris, 1925. Newspapers say the tower is rusting and costly to maintain.
Con man Victor Lustig reads this and has an idea.
He poses as a government official and invites scrap metal dealers to a fancy hotel.

Lustig even hints he'd accept a bribe, which makes him look like a real official.
Poisson pays. Lustig takes the money and flees to Vienna.

What if the richest woman in America refused to pay for hot oatmeal?
Meet Hetty Green, nicknamed the Witch of Wall Street.

Her method was simple: buy when everyone panics, and keep lots of cash.
