But she was famously cheap.
Stories say she wore the same black dress for years, and ate her oatmeal cold to avoid heating it.
Guinness once listed her as the world's greatest miser.
The darkest legend says she delayed a doctor for her son's injured leg, though historians debate it.
Her investing was brilliant. Her spending, painful.
Money is a tool. Hoarding it all is not the same as living well.
What if one man made a fortune while the whole market crashed?
Jesse Livermore started at fourteen, writing stock prices on a board in Boston.
He noticed patterns, and began betting on them.
By his thirties, he had won and lost fortunes. More than once.
In 1929, everyone believed prices could only go up.
Livermore didn't. He bet that stocks would fall.
When the crash came in October, his bets paid off, reportedly around a hundred million dollars.
Suddenly he was one of the richest men in America, and one of the most hated.
But he kept making huge, risky bets.
By 1934, he was bankrupt again.
Being right once can make you rich. Staying rich takes discipline.
What if the worst decision of Warren Buffett's life came from being annoyed?
In 1962, Buffett starts buying shares of Berkshire Hathaway, a struggling textile mill.
The plan: buy cheap, then sell the shares back to the company for a quick profit.
The boss, Seabury Stanton, agrees on eleven dollars fifty a share.
But the official offer arrives at eleven thirty-seven and a half. An eighth of a dollar less.
Buffett is furious. So he buys more shares, takes control, and fires Stanton.
Now he owns a dying textile business.
For twenty years, it keeps losing money.
Buffett later called it his two hundred billion dollar mistake.
He built an empire anyway, using Berkshire to buy insurance companies.
The lesson? Revenge is a terrible investment strategy.
What if a company invented the thing that would destroy it, and then hid it?
In the seventies, Kodak sells most of the film in America.
Every photo means film to buy and prints to develop. A money machine.
In 1975, a young Kodak engineer, Steven Sasson, builds the first digital camera.
It weighs about eight pounds and takes twenty-three seconds to save one tiny black and white photo.
His bosses' reaction, as he remembers it: that's cute, but don't tell anyone.
Why? Digital photos don't need film. And film is where Kodak makes its money.
So Kodak keeps selling film, while others build digital cameras, then phones.
In 2012, Kodak files for bankruptcy.
It saw the future first, and looked away.
If you don't replace your own product, someone else will.
What if you could have bought Netflix for fifty million dollars, and laughed instead?
It's 2000. Blockbuster is the king of video rentals, with thousands of stores.
Netflix is a tiny company mailing DVDs, and it's losing money.
Its founders fly to Dallas and offer to sell Netflix to Blockbuster for fifty million dollars.
According to Netflix co-founder Marc Randolph, Blockbuster's boss could barely stop laughing.
Why buy them? Blockbuster made a fortune from late fees alone.
But Netflix had no late fees. Then it moved to streaming.
Customers stopped driving to stores.
In 2010, Blockbuster filed for bankruptcy.
Today, Netflix is worth hundreds of billions of dollars.
The scariest competitor is the one that looks too small to matter.
What if you turned down forty-four billion dollars, then sold for about five billion?
In the nineties, Yahoo is the front door of the internet.
In 1998, Google's founders reportedly offer to sell their search engine to Yahoo for about a million dollars.
Yahoo passes.
In 2006, Yahoo tries to buy Facebook for a billion. The deal falls apart.
Then, in 2008, Microsoft offers forty-four point six billion dollars for Yahoo.
That's sixty-two percent above its stock price.
Yahoo's board says no. Too low.
Meanwhile, Google and Facebook grow into giants.
In 2017, Yahoo's main business is sold to Verizon for about four and a half billion.
Sometimes the best offer is the one you're about to refuse.
What if Apple only survived because its biggest rival saved it?
1997. Apple is losing money fast. Steve Jobs later said it was about ninety days from going broke.
Jobs has just returned to the company he co-founded.
And he makes a shocking deal with his rival, Bill Gates.
Microsoft invests a hundred and fifty million dollars in Apple.
It also promises to keep making Microsoft Office for the Mac.
At a Mac conference, Gates appears on a giant screen. The crowd boos.
But the money and the software buy Apple time.
Then come the iMac, the iPod, and the iPhone.
Apple becomes one of the most valuable companies in the world.
Sometimes your rival is worth more to you alive than dead.
What if the world's biggest Bitcoin exchange started as a site for trading game cards?
Mt. Gox stands for Magic: The Gathering Online eXchange.
In 2010, it's turned into a Bitcoin exchange, run from Tokyo.
By 2013, it handles most of the world's Bitcoin trading.
But behind the scenes, coins have been quietly disappearing for years.
In February 2014, withdrawals suddenly stop.
About eight hundred fifty thousand bitcoins are missing.
Some two hundred thousand are later found in an old wallet.
Customers wait ten years before the first repayments start.
The lesson? Coins left on an exchange are only as safe as the exchange.
Not your keys, not your coins.
What if a thirty-two billion dollar company vanished in about a week?
FTX is a crypto exchange founded in 2019 by Sam Bankman-Fried.
By early 2022, it's valued at thirty-two billion dollars, with Super Bowl ads and celebrity fans.
In November 2022, a news report reveals that its sister firm, Alameda, is propped up by FTX's own token.
Then a rival exchange announces it's dumping that token.
Panic. Customers rush to withdraw billions in just a few days.
But the money isn't there. Customer deposits had been secretly used by Alameda.
On November eleventh, FTX files for bankruptcy.
In 2024, Bankman-Fried is sentenced to twenty-five years in prison.
Famous ads and a huge valuation prove nothing.
If you can't see where your money is, assume you don't know.
What if a coin designed to always be worth one dollar dropped to almost nothing?
TerraUSD is a stablecoin. One coin is supposed to equal one dollar.
But there's no dollar in a vault behind it. Just an algorithm and a sister coin, Luna.
The idea: if the price slips, the system swaps it for newly created Luna, to push it back up.
And a savings app on Terra pays almost twenty percent a year. Billions pour in.
In May 2022, big withdrawals push TerraUSD below one dollar.
The system creates more and more Luna to defend the peg.
Luna floods the market, and its price collapses.
Within days, Luna goes from around eighty dollars to a tiny fraction of a cent.
About forty billion dollars in value disappears.
When something promises safety and twenty percent, ask what's really holding it up.
What if a bank collapsed in under two days because of a group chat?
Silicon Valley Bank is the bank of tech startups.
In 2020 and 2021, deposits pour in, and the bank invests them in safe long-term government bonds.
Safe, unless interest rates rise. And in 2022, they rise fast.
New bonds pay more, so the old ones lose value. The bank is sitting on huge hidden losses.
On March eighth, 2023, it announces a loss and asks for new money.
Founders text each other: get your money out.
The next day, customers try to withdraw forty-two billion dollars.
On March tenth, regulators shut the bank down.
Most deposits were above the two hundred fifty thousand dollar insurance limit.
A bank runs on trust. And trust can now leave at the speed of a text.
What if people queued for hours outside a bank, just to get their own money back?
Northern Rock is a fast-growing British mortgage bank.
It even offers loans worth up to a hundred and twenty-five percent of a home's value.
To fund all that lending, it borrows short-term money from other banks, again and again.
In August 2007, that money suddenly dries up. Banks stop trusting each other.
Northern Rock asks the Bank of England for emergency help.
The news comes out. And people do the logical thing: they rush to the bank.
Long queues form outside branches across the country.
It's the first run on a British bank in more than a century.
The government guarantees deposits, and in 2008, takes over the bank.
A bank can be fine on paper and still fall, if it can't borrow tomorrow.
What if a nine billion dollar company was built on a machine that didn't really work?
In 2003, nineteen-year-old Elizabeth Holmes drops out of Stanford to start Theranos.
The promise: hundreds of medical tests from just a few drops of blood.
Investors love it. Former cabinet secretaries join the board.
By 2014, Theranos is valued at nine billion dollars.
But inside, the machine keeps failing.
Most tests are secretly run on regular lab machines bought from other companies.
In 2015, a Wall Street Journal reporter exposes the truth.
The value goes to zero. In 2022, Holmes is convicted of defrauding investors.
Big names on the board did not check the science.
Before you invest, ask to see it work. Not just hear it work.
What if you could buy stocks with mostly borrowed money? In 1929, millions did.
The twenties are roaring. Cars, radios, electricity. Stocks only seem to go up.
You can buy shares with as little as ten percent of your own money. The broker lends the rest.
In September 1929, the Dow hits a record: three hundred eighty-one.
Then prices start slipping. And brokers demand their money back.
To pay, investors are forced to sell. Which pushes prices lower. Which forces more selling.
On October twenty-eighth and twenty-ninth, the market falls more than twenty percent in two days.
By 1932, the Dow is down about eighty-nine percent.
Thousands of banks fail. One American worker in four loses their job.
The Dow won't get back to its 1929 peak until 1954. Twenty-five years later.
Borrowed money makes the ride faster, in both directions.
What if a shoeshine boy saved a man from the 1929 crash?
Joseph Kennedy, father of a future president, is a wealthy investor on Wall Street.
One day in 1929, he stops to get his shoes shined.
And the boy starts giving him stock tips.
As the story goes, Kennedy thinks: if even shoeshine boys are betting on stocks, there's nobody left to buy.
So he sells much of his stock.
Months later, the market crashes. Kennedy keeps his fortune.
Historians say the story may be polished, but the idea stuck.
In 1934, Kennedy becomes the first boss of the new market watchdog, the SEC.
Today, people still talk about the shoeshine signal.
When everyone around you is giving stock tips, it might be time to be careful.
What if a five dollar stuffed toy became a retirement plan?
In the late nineties, America goes crazy for Beanie Babies.
They cost about five dollars in shops. But the maker has a trick.
It retires designs without warning. Suddenly, a toy is rare.
Collectors buy them as investments. Price guides predict values for years ahead.
Some sell for hundreds, even thousands of dollars on a new website called eBay.
In one Las Vegas divorce, a judge reportedly split a couple's collection on the courtroom floor.
But there's a problem: everyone is keeping them in mint condition. Millions of them.
Nothing is rare if everybody hoards it.
Around 1999, the craze fades and prices crash. Most are worth a few dollars today.
Scarcity created by marketing is not the same as real value.
What if people bought land in Florida without ever seeing it, and some of it was underwater?
In the 1920s, cars and new roads make Florida the dream destination.
Land prices start climbing. Then they explode.
Buyers only need about ten percent down to reserve a lot.
So traders called binder boys flip those reservations, sometimes several times in a single day.
Many buyers never visit. Some lots turn out to be swamp.
In late 1925, railways stop carrying non-essential freight. Building materials can't get in.
Then a ship capsizes and blocks Miami's harbor.
In 1926, buyers vanish, and a deadly hurricane hits Miami.
The boom is over. Many lots are worth a fraction of their price.
If something is selling too fast to even look at it, slow down.
What if one palace garden in Tokyo was said to be worth more than all of California?
In the late 1980s, Japan's economy looks unstoppable.
Interest rates are low, and banks lend freely, using land as collateral.
Higher land prices mean bigger loans. Bigger loans buy more land.
At the peak, a popular estimate said the Imperial Palace grounds were worth more than all the real estate in California.
Japanese companies buy famous American icons, like New York's Rockefeller Center.
On December twenty-ninth, 1989, the Nikkei stock index hits almost thirty-nine thousand.
Then the central bank raises interest rates to cool things down.
By 1992, the Nikkei has lost about sixty percent. Land prices keep falling for years.
Japan calls the next decade the lost decade.
When prices only make sense if they keep rising, they usually stop.
What if you invested at the top, and had to wait thirty-four years just to break even?
December 1989. Japan's Nikkei index closes at a record: almost thirty-nine thousand.
Investors are sure Japan will soon lead the world.
Stocks are priced at around sixty times their profits. Very expensive.
Then the bubble bursts.
In 2009, after another global crisis, the Nikkei falls near seven thousand. Down more than eighty percent.
A whole generation of Japanese savers learns to fear stocks.
It isn't until February 2024 that the Nikkei finally beats its 1989 record.
Thirty-four years later.
Dividends helped a bit along the way. But buying everything in one expensive market was brutal.
Long term only works if you don't overpay, and you don't put everything in one place.
What if your great-grandparents had bought just one share of Coca-Cola in 1919?
That year, Coca-Cola goes public at forty dollars a share.
Within a year, sugar prices spike, and the stock drops to about nineteen dollars. Ouch.
Most people would sell. But imagine they forgot about it in a drawer.
Over the decades, the company splits its shares again and again.
That one share becomes nine thousand two hundred sixteen shares.
Today, that's worth well over six hundred thousand dollars.
And it pays roughly eighteen thousand dollars a year in dividends.
If every dividend had been reinvested, estimates run into the millions.
All from one share, and a lot of patience.
Time in a good business can do more than any clever trade.
What if a retired tax auditor turned five thousand dollars into twenty-two million?
Anne Scheiber worked at the IRS for over twenty years. She had a law degree, but she says she was never promoted.
In 1944, she retires with about five thousand dollars in savings.
She invests it in stocks of big, well-known companies. Drinks, medicine, entertainment.
Then she does something rare: almost nothing.
She keeps the stocks, reinvests the dividends, and lives in a tiny rented apartment.
She reads annual reports and goes to shareholder meetings.
When she dies in 1995, at a hundred and one, her portfolio is worth about twenty-two million dollars.
That's roughly eighteen percent a year, for fifty years.
She leaves almost all of it to fund scholarships for young women.
Patience is a strategy anyone can afford.
What if a secretary quietly copied her boss's investments for sixty years?
Sylvia Bloom works as a legal secretary at a big New York law firm for sixty-seven years.
She takes the subway to work, even in her nineties.
Part of her job: placing stock orders for her bosses.
So when a boss buys a stock, she buys the same one. Just a much smaller amount.
She never talks about it. Not even her family knows.
She dies in 2016, at ninety-six.
Her niece opens the accounts and finds about eight point two million dollars.
Sylvia leaves more than six million to a charity that helps poor students go to college.
It's the biggest gift from a single person in its history.
Small amounts, good companies, and a lot of time. No secret formula.
What if the famous line, seventy percent of lottery winners go broke, was never backed by research?
You've probably heard it. It's everywhere online.
But the foundation often cited as its source later said it couldn't back up that number.
So what do real studies say?
In Florida, researchers found that people who won fifty to a hundred fifty thousand dollars were about as likely to go bankrupt a few years later as people who won very little.
A medium win often just delayed money problems.
But in Sweden, a large study found that big winners mostly stayed richer, for many years.
The pattern: a one-time win doesn't change habits. Spending can quietly rise to match.
And the odds of hitting the Powerball jackpot? About one in two hundred ninety-two million.
Buying tickets as a plan to get rich is a losing bet.
The real jackpot is a habit, not a ticket.
What if a soda ad offered a fighter jet, and someone actually tried to claim it?
In 1996, Pepsi runs a points campaign. Drink Pepsi, collect points, swap them for T-shirts and jackets.
At the end of the TV ad, as a joke, a Harrier fighter jet appears: seven million Pepsi points.
A twenty-one-year-old student, John Leonard, reads the rules.
You can buy extra points for ten cents each.
Seven million points is about seven hundred thousand dollars. A Harrier jet costs tens of millions.
So he gathers investors, and mails Pepsi a check for seven hundred thousand dollars.
Pepsi says no. It was a joke. Leonard sues.
In 1999, a judge rules that no reasonable person would take the ad as a real offer.
No jet. But the story becomes legend.
Always read the fine print. Especially the fun print.
What if a soda company briefly owned submarines and warships?
In 1959, at a fair in Moscow, Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev tastes Pepsi.
Years later, Pepsi wants to sell in the Soviet Union. But there's a problem.
Soviet money, the ruble, can't be used outside the country.
So they trade. Pepsi syrup in, Soviet vodka out, to sell in America.
In 1989, the Soviets need a bigger deal. So they pay with what they have.
Seventeen old submarines, a cruiser, a frigate, and a destroyer.
Pepsi sells them for scrap metal.
Its boss reportedly joked to a White House adviser: we're disarming the Soviet Union faster than you are.
When money doesn't work, people still find a way to trade.
Money is just a tool for swapping things. Sometimes, the things are warships.
What if a giant fraud was hiding inside tanks of salad oil?
In the early sixties, Tino De Angelis runs a vegetable oil company in New Jersey.
He borrows huge sums, using the oil in his tanks as collateral.
Inspectors come to check. They dip a stick in the tanks, and see oil.
But the tanks are mostly filled with water. Oil floats on top, so only the top looks right.
Some tanks are even connected by pipes, so the same oil can be moved around to fool inspectors.
In 1963, the scheme collapses. The missing oil is worth about a hundred and fifty million dollars.
Lenders lose fortunes. American Express is caught up in it, and its stock falls by about half.
A young investor named Warren Buffett studies the mess, and buys a big stake in American Express.
It becomes one of his best investments.
Check what's under the surface. And remember: panic can create bargains.
What if a world-changing technology still made most of its early investors lose money?
Britain, the 1840s. Railways are the new miracle. Travel that took days now takes hours.
Everyone wants a piece. New railway companies appear every week.
In 1846 alone, Parliament approves more than two hundred and seventy new railway lines.
Investors include Charles Darwin and the Brontë sisters.
The star is George Hudson, nicknamed the Railway King.
But some of his companies pay dividends using new investors' money, not real profits.
In 1847, interest rates rise, money gets tight, and railway shares crash.
Many planned lines are never built. Hudson's tricks are exposed.
Yet the tracks that were built changed Britain forever.
A technology can be revolutionary, and still be a terrible investment at the wrong price.
What if your bank opened accounts in your name, without asking you?
Wells Fargo is one of America's biggest banks.
Its motto for selling: eight is great. The goal is eight products per customer.
Employees face tough daily sales targets. Miss them, and you could lose your job.
So some start opening accounts and credit cards that customers never asked for.
Customers notice strange fees, and cards they never ordered.
In 2016, regulators reveal it. Later estimates reach up to three and a half million fake accounts.
Thousands of employees are fired, and the CEO resigns.
In 2020, the bank agrees to pay three billion dollars to settle the case.
The targets created the fraud they were supposed to measure.
Check your bank statements. Every line.
What if cars were smart enough to know when they were being tested?
Volkswagen sells clean diesel cars. Powerful, efficient, and green, says the ads.
But a small team of university researchers tests them on real roads.
Some emit up to forty times the legal limit of a harmful gas.
In the lab, the numbers were perfect. How?
Hidden software detects a test. Then the car switches to a clean mode. On the road, it doesn't bother.
In September 2015, US regulators go public. About eleven million cars worldwide have the software.
Volkswagen's stock loses about a third of its value in two days.
The CEO resigns. Fines, buybacks and settlements add up to more than thirty billion euros.
A reputation built over decades, damaged in a week.
Trust is an asset. Lose it, and the market sends the bill.
What if the company that sold almost half the world's smartphones lost it all in six years?
In 2007, Nokia is the king of phones. Tough, cheap, with batteries that last for days.
That year, a new phone appears with a big touchscreen and almost no buttons.
Nokia's engineers aren't worried. Their phones are tougher and the battery lasts longer.
But the new phones aren't really about calls. They're about apps.
Developers build apps for the new platforms, not for Nokia's old system.
In 2011, Nokia's new boss writes that the company is standing on a burning platform.
In 2013, Nokia sells its phone business to Microsoft for about seven billion dollars.
At its peak, Nokia had been worth around two hundred fifty billion.
Being the best at yesterday's game doesn't win tomorrow's.
Market leaders fall when they defend what they have, instead of what customers want next.
What if one of the best stocks in history first lost ninety-four percent of its value?
December 1999. Amazon is an internet star, selling books online. Its stock is near a hundred dollars.
Then the dot-com bubble bursts.
By late 2001, Amazon's stock is around six dollars. Down about ninety-four percent.
Jeff Bezos starts his letter to shareholders with one word: Ouch.
Hundreds of internet companies go bankrupt. Many people think Amazon is next.
But Amazon keeps growing its sales, cutting costs, and building warehouses.
Years later, it adds cloud computing, which becomes a money machine.
Today, Amazon is worth trillions of dollars.
But to enjoy that, you had to survive watching ninety-four percent disappear. Almost nobody did.
Great investments rarely feel great while you hold them.
What if one confusing decision wiped out three quarters of a company's value in a few months?
July 2011. Netflix offers DVDs by mail and streaming, together, for about ten dollars a month.
Then it splits them into two plans. Keeping both now costs about sixteen dollars. A sixty percent jump.
Customers are angry. Then, in September, it gets stranger.
Netflix announces the DVD service will become a separate company, with a new name: Qwikster.
Two websites. Two accounts. Two bills.
And the Twitter name Qwikster already belongs to someone else, a guy with a picture of a puppet smoking.
Three weeks later, Netflix cancels Qwikster.
About eight hundred thousand subscribers leave. The stock falls roughly seventy-five percent from its summer high.
The CEO apologizes. Netflix recovers, and goes on to dominate streaming.
Change can be right, and still fail if customers feel ignored.
What if a famous toy store died, not because people stopped buying toys, but because of debt?
Toys R Us is a giant. For decades, it's the place kids beg to visit.
In 2005, investment firms buy the company for about six point six billion dollars.
But they pay mostly with borrowed money. And that debt is put on Toys R Us itself.
Now the company owes around five billion dollars, and pays roughly four hundred million in interest every year.
Money that could have fixed stores or built a great website goes to lenders instead.
Meanwhile, Amazon and Walmart sell toys cheaper and faster.
In 2017, Toys R Us files for bankruptcy.
In 2018, its American stores close. Tens of thousands of jobs disappear.
The toys were still selling. The debt was the problem.
Debt doesn't care if you're famous. It just wants to be paid.
What if the US government could solve a crisis with one coin worth a trillion dollars?
In America, Congress sets a limit on how much the government can borrow: the debt ceiling.
Every few years, politicians fight over raising it. If they don't, the country could miss payments on its debt.
Then someone notices a strange detail in the law.
The Treasury is allowed to mint platinum coins of any value. The rule was meant for collector coins.
So the idea is: mint one platinum coin worth one trillion dollars.
Deposit it at the central bank, and spend the money without borrowing more.
It sounds like a joke, but serious economists debated it in 2013 and again in 2023.
Treasury and the central bank shot it down. Too risky, and against the spirit of the law.
But it shows something real: money is a rule we agree on.
A coin is worth what the system says it's worth. Trust does the rest.
What if a cryptocurrency made as a joke became worth more than many big companies?
In 2013, two software engineers create Dogecoin, using a famous meme of a Shiba Inu dog.
The goal: make fun of the crypto craze.
Fans love it. They use it to tip each other online, and even help send Jamaica's bobsled team to the Winter Olympics.
Unlike Bitcoin, there's no limit. About five billion new coins are created every year.
For years, one coin is worth a fraction of a cent.
Then in 2021, a billionaire keeps tweeting about it. The price explodes.
In May 2021, Dogecoin hits about seventy cents. Its total value tops eighty billion dollars.
Days later, he jokes about it on live TV, and the price falls hard.
A joke can move markets. But hype without value tends to fade.
If you buy a meme, be ready to laugh, or cry.
What if making a coin cost almost four times what it's worth?
Meet the American penny. One cent.
In 2024, the US Mint says each penny cost about three point seven cents to make and ship.
So every new penny lost money before anyone spent it.
That year, pennies cost the government about eighty-five million dollars in losses.
And the nickel is even worse: about fourteen cents to make a five cent coin.
Meanwhile, many pennies just sit in jars, drawers, and couch cushions.
Canada stopped making its penny in 2012. Prices are simply rounded to the nearest five cents.
In 2025, the US finally stopped making new pennies too. Old ones still work.
Money is supposed to be worth more than it costs to make. When it isn't, it's time to change.
Even the smallest coin follows the rules of economics.
What if a monk who was friends with Leonardo da Vinci wrote the rules every company still follows?
Venice, 1494. Luca Pacioli, a monk and math teacher, publishes a giant math book.
Inside, a few pages explain how Venetian merchants keep their accounts.
He didn't invent the method. But he was the first to print it clearly, for anyone to learn.
The idea is simple: every transaction is written twice.
Sell a cloth for ten ducats? Your cash goes up ten. Your stock of cloth goes down ten.
One side is called debit, the other credit. At the end, both sides must balance.
If they don't, there's a mistake, or a theft.
The book spreads across Europe. Pacioli also teaches math to his friend Leonardo.
Five hundred years later, every bank, startup and giant company still uses double entry.
Every euro comes from somewhere and goes somewhere. Track both.
What if one of the most famous stories in finance was mostly made up?
The legend: June 1815, the Battle of Waterloo.
Banker Nathan Rothschild supposedly learns of Britain's victory first, maybe by carrier pigeon.
He pretends to sell British bonds. Everyone panics and sells. Then he secretly buys it all cheap.
A giant fortune in one day. Great story.
But historians say it doesn't hold up.
It was spread decades later, in an 1846 pamphlet written to attack the family, with no real evidence.
Rothschild did get early news through his couriers. But historians found no sign of a huge win that day.
Some even think the war's sudden end hurt his business. And there were no pigeons.
Stories about all-knowing insiders spread fast, because they feel true.
Before believing a market legend, ask one question: what's the source?
What if your money was a giant stone that never moved, and one sat at the bottom of the sea?
On the island of Yap, in the Pacific, people used huge stone discs called rai.
They were carved on another island hundreds of kilometers away, and brought back by canoe.
Some are taller than a person and weigh several tonnes.
So how do you pay with one? You don't move it.
Everyone simply agrees that it now belongs to someone else. The whole village remembers who owns what.
One story says a stone sank during the trip home. It was never seen again.
But everyone agreed it existed. So it stayed valuable, and could still be traded.
Later, a sea captain brought in more stones with modern ships, and the newer ones were worth less.
Value came from effort, rarity, and shared memory. A bit like a ledger.
Money isn't the object. It's the agreement about who owns what.
What if, in a prison camp with no money, people invented their own currency?
World War Two. In a prison camp for soldiers, a young British economist, R. A. Radford, watches what happens.
Prisoners receive Red Cross parcels: chocolate, jam, tea, and cigarettes.
Not everyone wants the same things. So they start trading.
Soon, one item becomes the money: the cigarette.
It's small, easy to count, easy to carry, and almost everyone accepts it. Even non-smokers.
Prices appear. A tin of jam might cost a set number of cigarettes.
When a big shipment arrives, there are suddenly more cigarettes, and prices go up. Inflation.
When supplies run low and people smoke them, prices fall.
Radford publishes his observations in 1945. It becomes a classic of economics.
Money isn't just made by governments. It appears wherever people need to trade.
What if the money in some American prisons was a pouch of fish?
Cash is banned in US federal prisons. For years, cigarettes did the job.
Then in 2004, federal prisons ban smoking. So prisoners need a new currency.
They choose the mack: a little pouch of mackerel from the prison shop, worth about a dollar.
Why mackerel? It keeps for a long time, its value is stable, and the guards don't want it.
With macks, you can pay for a haircut, laundry, or someone to clean your cell.
Some prisoners hardly eat them. They just collect them, like savings.
Later, a researcher found that in some prisons, ramen noodles started to replace mackerel.
As prison meals got worse, the most wanted food became the money.
The best money is something many people want, that's easy to store and hard to fake.
Even behind bars, the rules of money are the same.
What if banknotes were worth less than the paper to make a handbag from them?
Venezuela has some of the largest oil reserves on Earth. Oil pays for almost everything.
In 2014, oil prices crash. The government's income collapses.
To keep paying, it prints more and more money.
Prices explode. In 2018, the central bank itself reports inflation of over one hundred thirty thousand percent.
A coffee could cost more by the time you finished it.
People stop counting cash. Shops weigh stacks of bills instead.
Street artists weave worthless notes into bags and sell them, for more than the notes are worth.
The government cuts zeros off the currency three times. Fourteen zeros in total.
Millions of people leave the country. Many who stay switch to US dollars.
When a government prints money to pay its bills, the people pay through prices.
What if prices doubled about every fifteen hours?
Hungary, 1946. The war has destroyed factories, bridges and railways.
The country must pay war reparations, and there's very little to buy.
The government prints money to keep going. Then prints faster.
In July 1946, prices rise by more than forty million billion percent in a single month.
It's the worst hyperinflation ever recorded.
Workers are paid twice a day, and run to spend their wages before lunch.
Banknotes get absurd: one hundred quintillion pengő on a single note. That's a one followed by twenty zeros.
Streets are covered with worthless paper money. Street cleaners sweep it up like leaves.
In August, Hungary launches a new currency, the forint. One forint equals four hundred octillion old pengő.
Money only works if people trust it will still be worth something tomorrow.
What if America's central bank was planned in secret, by bankers pretending to go duck hunting?
In 1907, a financial panic hits the US. Banks fail, and there's no central bank to help.
The banker J.P. Morgan locks other bankers in his library until they agree to rescue the system.
Everyone agrees: the country can't depend on one rich man every time.
In November 1910, a senator and a few top bankers board a private train car at night.
They tell reporters they're going duck hunting. Some use only first names, to stay unrecognized.
Their destination: a private club on Jekyll Island, off the coast of Georgia.
For about ten days, they draft a plan for a central banking system.
Their plan isn't passed as is, but it shapes the law that follows.
In 1913, the Federal Reserve is created. The secret trip was only told publicly years later.
Big institutions often start in small rooms. Knowing their history helps you understand them.
What if one TV speech on a Sunday night changed the meaning of money?
After World War Two, the world agrees on a system: the US dollar is tied to gold.
Foreign governments can swap thirty-five dollars for one ounce of American gold.
But by the late sixties, the US is printing more dollars than its gold can cover. War and spending pile up.
Some countries get nervous, and start trading in their dollars for gold.
American gold reserves keep shrinking.
On August fifteenth, 1971, President Nixon interrupts Sunday evening TV.
He announces that dollars can no longer be swapped for gold. Temporarily, he says.
It never comes back. From then on, the dollar is backed by trust in the US government, not by metal.
Gold, once fixed at thirty-five dollars an ounce, later climbs to thousands.
Today's money is a promise. Its value depends on how well that promise is kept.
What if the government ordered you to hand over your gold, or risk ten years in prison?
1933. The Great Depression. Thousands of banks have failed. People are hoarding gold.
In April, President Franklin Roosevelt signs an order.
Americans must turn in most of their gold coins, bars and gold certificates to the Federal Reserve.
They get paid twenty dollars and sixty-seven cents per ounce, in paper money.
Some exceptions: jewelry, rare collector coins, and a small amount per person.
The penalty for refusing: up to ten thousand dollars, and up to ten years in prison.
Then in 1934, the government raises the official price of gold to thirty-five dollars.
Gold that people handed in at twenty dollars sixty-seven is suddenly worth about seventy percent more.
Owning gold bars stays illegal for most Americans until 1975.
In a crisis, the rules about what you own can change overnight.
What if a tiny country let its giant banks fail, and sent bankers to prison?
Iceland has about three hundred thousand people. Fishing, geysers, and quiet towns.
But in the 2000s, its three biggest banks grow fast. Very fast.
They borrow abroad and expand everywhere. Their assets reach about ten times the size of Iceland's economy.
They even attract savers in Britain and the Netherlands with high-interest online accounts.
In October 2008, the global crisis hits. In about a week, all three banks collapse.
The Icelandic króna loses around half its value. Prices jump, and many families struggle.
The government protects local savings accounts, but lets the banks fail instead of saving them with public money.
A special prosecutor investigates. Dozens of bankers are convicted, and many go to prison.
Within a few years, the economy recovers, helped by a tourism boom.
When banks grow bigger than their country, someone eventually pays. Ask who, before it happens.
What if you woke up one morning and could only take sixty euros a day out of your own bank account?
Greece, 2015. After years of crisis, the country is deep in debt, and talks with its lenders break down.
The government calls a referendum on the lenders' demands. Savers panic and pull out their cash.
On June twenty-ninth, the banks don't open.
They stay closed for three weeks. ATMs work, but each person can take out only sixty euros a day.
Sending money abroad is blocked. Businesses struggle to pay foreign suppliers.
Pensioners queue in front of banks just to get part of their pension.
In the vote, about sixty-one percent say no to the lenders' terms.
A week later, the government accepts a new bailout anyway, worth about eighty-six billion euros.
Some limits on money stay in place for four years, until 2019.
Money in a bank is a promise. In a crisis, access to it can be limited.
What if your country had five presidents in two weeks, and froze your bank account?
In the nineties, Argentina ties its peso to the US dollar. One peso equals one dollar.
For a while, it works. Inflation disappears.
But the economy slows, debt piles up, and people start to doubt the promise.
Savers rush to withdraw their money, especially dollars.
On December first, 2001, the government limits withdrawals to two hundred fifty pesos a week. People call it the corralito, the little fence.
Protests explode. The president leaves the presidential palace by helicopter.
Argentina goes through five presidents in about two weeks, and stops paying its foreign debt.
In 2002, the peg breaks. The peso loses about three quarters of its value.
Many savers' dollar deposits are converted into pesos at a bad rate. Years of savings shrink.
A fixed exchange rate is only as strong as the trust behind it.
What if, to rescue your bank, part of your savings was simply taken?
Cyprus, 2013. A small island country with a huge banking sector.
Its two biggest banks lost billions when Greek government bonds were cut in value.
Europe agrees to help, but with a condition: savers must pay part of the bill.
The first plan proposes a tax on every bank account, even small ones. Parliament rejects it.
Meanwhile, banks close for nearly two weeks. ATMs limit withdrawals.
The final deal: accounts under a hundred thousand euros are protected.
But above that, savers at the biggest bank lose almost half of the extra amount, turned into bank shares.
At the second bank, which is closed down, big depositors lose even more.
It's the first time Europe makes savers help rescue a bank. It's called a bail-in.
Deposit protection has limits. Know the limit for your account.
What if one of the world's biggest insurance markets started in a coffee shop?
London, around 1688. Edward Lloyd opens a coffee house near the river.
Ship captains, merchants and sailors gather there to drink coffee and trade news.
Lloyd posts the latest shipping news. Which ships arrived, which sank, which pirates are out there.
Sending a ship across the ocean is a huge gamble. A storm can wipe out a fortune.
So wealthy customers offer a deal. Pay me a fee, and if your ship sinks, I'll cover part of the loss.
They sign their names under the description of the voyage. That's where the word underwriter comes from.
Spreading the risk among many people makes long voyages possible.
Lloyd's coffee house grows into Lloyd's of London, still a major insurance market today.
Insurance turns a disaster that could ruin one person into a small cost shared by many.
You can't avoid every storm. But you can share the risk.
What if the modern payment card was born because a businessman forgot his wallet at dinner?
New York, 1949. Frank McNamara finishes a business dinner and realizes he has no wallet.
That's the story the company would tell for decades. Historians say it was polished for marketing.
Either way, McNamara has an idea: a card you can use instead of cash at many restaurants.
In 1950, he launches the Diners Club card, made of cardboard.
At first, it works at about two dozen restaurants in New York, for a few hundred members.
Restaurants pay a small fee on each meal, about seven percent, but get new customers.
Members get one bill each month and pay it all at once.
Within a year, the club has about twenty thousand members.
Banks soon copy the idea. That's how the credit card industry is born.
Paying later feels easy. That's exactly why the bill always comes.
What if your PIN has four digits because of one inventor's wife?
London, 1960s. Banks close in the afternoon and on weekends. No cash after hours.
Engineer John Shepherd-Barron thinks: if a machine can sell chocolate, why not cash?
On June twenty-seventh, 1967, the first cash machine opens outside a Barclays bank in north London.
There are no plastic cards yet. You insert a special paper voucher, marked with a slightly radioactive substance so the machine can read it.
Then you type a code, and get a fixed ten pounds.
A famous TV comedy actor is the first to try it.
Shepherd-Barron later said he wanted a six-digit code, but his wife could only remember four.
So four digits became the standard. Or so the story goes.
Today there are millions of cash machines around the world.
Convenience changes how we spend. Easier cash, easier spending.
What if the world's most famous money game was invented to warn people against greed?
In 1904, a woman named Lizzie Magie patents a board game: The Landlord's Game.
She wants to show a problem: landlords collect rent and get richer, while tenants slowly go broke.
Her game even has two sets of rules.
In one, players try to crush each other with monopolies. In the other, wealth is shared, and everyone gains.
The crush-your-rivals version is the one people love.
Players make homemade copies for years, adding their own street names.
In the 1930s, a man named Charles Darrow sells a version to a big toy company, and it's sold as his invention.
The game becomes Monopoly. Darrow becomes a millionaire.
The company buys Magie's patent for about five hundred dollars. Her name is forgotten for decades.
A game about the unfairness of monopolies made its biggest fortune for someone else.
What if the New York Stock Exchange started under a tree?
New York, 1792. The new United States has issued government bonds, and people trade them in the street.
Earlier that year, a speculator's collapse caused a panic, and trust in traders fell.
On May seventeenth, twenty-four brokers meet under a buttonwood tree on Wall Street.
They sign a short agreement. Just two sentences.
Rule one: they will trade mainly with each other.
Rule two: they will charge the same commission: a quarter of a percent.
Simple rules, but they create a trusted club of traders.
A year later, they move indoors, to a coffee house. In 1817, they formalize their exchange.
It grows into the New York Stock Exchange, the biggest stock market in the world.
Markets don't just need money. They need rules people trust.
What if none of the original companies in America's most famous stock index were still in it?
1896. Journalist Charles Dow creates an index to show how the stock market is doing.
He picks twelve big industrial companies. Sugar, tobacco, cotton oil, leather, rubber, gas.
The math is simple: add up their stock prices, then divide by twelve. Done by hand.
The very first value: about forty-one.
Over the years, companies are replaced as the economy changes.
Leather and cotton oil give way to cars, then computers, then software.
The last original member, General Electric, is removed in 2018.
Today the Dow is above forty thousand, made of companies that didn't exist in 1896.
The index survives because it keeps replacing the losers.
Betting on one company is risky. Betting on the economy changing has worked better.
What if doubling your workers' pay made your company richer?
1913. Henry Ford's car factory has a problem. Work on the assembly line is boring and exhausting.
Workers quit constantly. To keep about fourteen thousand people, Ford has to hire around fifty thousand in a year.
In January 1914, Ford announces a shock: five dollars a day, for an eight-hour day.
That's about double the usual wage.
The next day, thousands of job seekers crowd outside the factory in freezing weather.
There's a catch: inspectors visit workers' homes to check they live the way Ford approves.
But it works. Workers stay, they get faster, and training costs fall.
Ford's profits rise. And his workers can now afford the cars they build.
Other companies are forced to raise wages too.
Paying people well can be a cost, or an investment. Ford bet on the second.
What if a court case from 1919 still shapes who companies work for?
By 1916, Ford Motor Company is swimming in cash, about sixty million dollars of extra profit.
Henry Ford decides: no more special dividends. He wants to build more factories, hire more workers and cut car prices.
But two shareholders object: the Dodge brothers, who own about ten percent of Ford.
They want their share of the profits, partly to build their own car company.
They sue. Ford tells the court he wants to spread the benefits to as many people as possible.
In 1919, the court sides with the Dodges.
It says a company exists mainly to make profits for its shareholders. Ford must pay a special dividend of about nineteen million dollars.
Furious, Ford buys out all the other shareholders, so no one can tell him what to do again.
The case is still debated today. Who should a company serve: owners, workers, or customers?
When you buy a share, you're one of the owners. That question becomes yours too.
What if the world's most famous burger chain was really a landlord?
In the 1950s, Ray Kroc is selling McDonald's franchises across America.
But franchise fees are small, and money is tight.
His finance chief, Harry Sonneborn, has an idea.
McDonald's should buy or lease the land under each restaurant.
Then rent it to the franchise owner, usually at a markup.
Now McDonald's earns rent every month, whether burgers sell well or not.
And it controls the best locations. If a franchisee breaks the rules, they can lose the building.
According to Kroc's own memoir, Sonneborn put it this way: we're not technically in the food business. We're in the real estate business.
Today, rent from franchisees is still one of McDonald's biggest sources of income.
Sometimes, the real business isn't what you sell. It's what you own.
What if your coffee shop was holding more customer money than many banks?
You load money onto a coffee chain's app or gift card. It's convenient, and you get rewards.
Now multiply that by millions of customers.
Starbucks holds well over a billion and a half dollars in money customers have loaded but not spent yet.
That's money it can use right away.
And unlike a bank, it pays you no interest on it.
It's like an interest-free loan from its own customers.
Even better for the company: some of that money is never spent. Forgotten cards, small leftover amounts.
Each year, the company counts part of these forgotten balances as revenue.
Loyalty apps aren't just about free coffee. They're also about holding your cash.
Before you preload money anywhere, ask who earns from holding it.
What if an airline's loyalty program was worth more than the airline itself?
In 1981, American Airlines launches a frequent flyer program. Fly more, earn miles, get free flights.
Soon, every airline copies it.
But the real money isn't in flights. It's in selling miles to banks.
Banks buy billions of miles to reward people who use their credit cards.
In 2020, during the pandemic, planes are empty. United Airlines borrows billions using its loyalty program as collateral.
Lenders value the program at around twenty-two billion dollars. At that moment, more than the whole airline on the stock market.
Miles act like a private currency. And the airline is its central bank.
It can create miles at will, and change how many you need for a flight. That's inflation.
Your miles can quietly lose value while you save them.
Points are money controlled by someone else. Spend them before they shrink.
What if building something yourself made you overpay for it?
In 2011, researchers ran a simple experiment.
Some people got a flat-pack storage box and assembled it themselves. Others got the same box, already built.
Then everyone was asked: how much would you pay for it?
The people who built it offered about sixty percent more.
Same box. Same quality. Just their own effort inside.
Another test: people folded paper origami.
They valued their own wobbly creations almost as much as ones made by experts. Strangers thought they were worth very little.
Researchers named it the IKEA effect: we overvalue what we built.
It also shows up in money: an investment you researched for hours, or a business you started. It's harder to let go.
Your effort isn't the same as value. Judge things as if someone else had built them.
What if a random number could change how much you're willing to pay?
In 1974, two psychologists spin a wheel of fortune in front of volunteers.
Secretly, the wheel is rigged to stop on either ten or sixty-five.
Then they ask: what percentage of African countries are in the United Nations?
People who saw ten guess about twenty-five percent on average. People who saw sixty-five guess about forty-five.
A meaningless number changed their answer. This is called anchoring.
Later experiments found that even the last digits of people's social security numbers influenced how much they bid for things.
Stores use this all the time. A crossed-out price of two hundred makes one hundred twenty feel cheap.
Or a very expensive item placed first on a menu makes everything else seem reasonable.
The first number you see sticks in your head, even when it shouldn't.
Before you decide what's a good price, ask: compared to what?
What if adding an option nobody wants made people spend more?
Economist Dan Ariely found a strange subscription offer from The Economist magazine.
Online only: fifty-nine dollars. Print only: one hundred twenty-five dollars. Print and online: also one hundred twenty-five dollars.
Who would choose print only, when print and online cost the same? Nobody.
He tested it on a hundred students. Sixteen chose online. Eighty-four chose print and online. Zero chose print only.
Then he removed the useless option.
Suddenly, sixty-eight chose the cheap online version. Only thirty-two picked the expensive one.
The useless option wasn't there to be chosen. It was there to make the expensive one look like a bargain.
It's called the decoy effect. You see it with popcorn sizes, coffee cups and phone plans.
The medium is often priced just close enough to the large to push you up.
When a choice looks obvious, check if an option was added just to steer you.
